text: Q-learning learns values and then acts on them. Policy gradient methods skip that middle step: they adjust the policy itself, nudging up the probability of actions that turned out well and nudging down those that turned out badly, much as a coach reinforces the movements that led a gymnast to a clean landing.

The policy is a network with parameters theta that outputs a probability for every action, usually through a softmax, exactly like a language model's distribution over the next token. The goal is to raise the expected return, called J of theta. The difficulty is that the return depends on actions that were sampled, and sampling a random choice has no derivative.

The way around it is the log-derivative trick. The gradient of the expected return equals the expected value of the return times the gradient of the log-probability of the actions that were taken. Everything in that expression can be computed from samples: run the policy, record what it did and what it earned, and for each action, step theta in the direction that makes that action more likely, scaled by how good the outcome was. This algorithm is called REINFORCE, published by Ronald Williams in nineteen ninety-two.

For a softmax policy, the gradient of a log-probability is wonderfully simple. With respect to the action scores, it is the one-hot vector of the chosen action minus the vector of probabilities. So a good outcome pushes the chosen action's score up and every other score down, each in proportion to how likely it was.

Plain REINFORCE is noisy, because the return of a single episode varies a great deal. The standard fix subtracts a baseline, such as the average return, from each return before scaling. That leaves the expected gradient unchanged, because the baseline does not depend on the action, but it greatly reduces the variance. Actions are now judged by whether they did better or worse than usual, a quantity called the advantage.

A large step on the strength of a few samples can wreck a good policy. Proximal policy optimisation, from Schulman and colleagues at OpenAI in twenty seventeen, limits each update by clipping the ratio between the new and the old probability of an action to a narrow band around one, so that no single batch can move the policy far. PPO, with a learned value function as its baseline, is the algorithm InstructGPT used for its reinforcement learning stage.

Seen this way, RLHF is a policy gradient on a very large policy: the language model samples a response, the reward model scores it, and the update raises the probability of the tokens in better than expected responses, with a leash to the reference model. That closes the module on reinforcement learning. Next come the capstones, beginning with a digit recogniser built from scratch in NumPy.
